content:
Two opposite claims circulate about Ezekiel 23 in Malaysia and Indonesia. Some Muslim speakers say that the Malay and Indonesian Bibles hide the chapter's explicit verses; some Christian readers say that the explicit wording quoted by Muslims is not in their Bible at all.[1]

Both claims can be checked, because the translations are published side by side. They differ, and the differences show translators making choices about the same Hebrew.

This article aims to provide context to those claims, insha'Allah, in five translation choices, read in six editions on the SABDA parallel Bible. For the Quran, Muslims hold that only the Arabic is the Quran, and al-Fārūqī calls its translations "mere aids to understanding it, not as text".[2] A reader of a Bible in Malay or Indonesian likewise holds a translation, and the comparison below shows how much a translation decides.

The editions compared here are the Indonesian Terjemahan Lama (TL, 1954), Terjemahan Baru (TB, 1974), Bahasa Indonesia Sehari-hari (BIS, 1985) and Alkitab Yang Terbuka (AYT, 2018), and the Malay Shellabear 2011 and Alkitab Versi Borneo (AVB, 2015).[3]

They follow different methods. TB, AYT, Shellabear and AVB keep close to the form of the Hebrew. BIS renders the meaning in everyday Indonesian. TL, the oldest, often uses words a modern reader finds indirect.

The Hebrew of 23:17 speaks of the Babylonians coming to Oholibah's "bed of love". TB keeps the image as tempat tidur percintaan, and Shellabear and AVB as ranjang percintaannya.[3]

BIS turns the image into the act it describes: Maka datanglah mereka dan tidur dengan dia, "then they came and slept with her". TL says the Babylonians came hendak berbuat zinah, "to commit adultery".[3] All three convey the same scene; only the formal versions keep the Hebrew picture.

Verse 20 is the one most often quoted. TB names the body directly, with auratnya and zakarnya, and AYT, Shellabear and AVB do the same, the last two with air mani.[3]

TL is less anatomical and uses dagingnya and cemarnya. BIS leaves the anatomy out altogether and speaks of desire: gejolak berahinya sebesar nafsu kuda jantan, "his passion as great as a stallion's lust".[3]

The difference in verse 20 is a difference of translation. The World English Bible renders the Hebrew word for word: the lovers' "flesh is as the flesh of donkeys, and whose issue is like the issue of horses".[4] TL keeps those same two words, daging and cemar, and TB and AVB name what they refer to.

A reader who meets the milder BIS has met a paraphrase. A reader who meets TB or AVB has met the Hebrew more nearly as it stands. The verse is in every edition.

It is often assumed that the Malay Bibles soften the text more than the Indonesian ones. The editions show otherwise. AVB, a Malay Bible of 2015, is as direct in verse 20 as TB, and more direct than the Indonesian TL and BIS.[3]

What decides the wording is the method of the translation and its date, and the line between Malay and Indonesian decides nothing. A quotation of "the Malay Bible" or "the Indonesian Bible" should therefore name its edition.

Bryan Bibb has argued that English translators often soften the sexual words of Ezekiel 16 and 23.[5] The same can be seen in BIS and TL, and it is visible to anyone who sets the editions side by side.

Nothing here is hidden. Each translation committee made a choice, and the choices are published. The claim that the verse has been removed, and the claim that Muslims invented it, both fail on the same page of SABDA.

The bottom line

Six Malay and Indonesian editions translate Ezekiel 23:17 and 23:20 in three ways: the formal versions keep the Hebrew images, BIS paraphrases them as desire, and TL uses older and less direct words. The explicit wording is in the Hebrew, in TB, AYT, Shellabear and AVB, and no edition removes the verse.

For a Muslim the comparison makes one point clear. The Quran is read in its Arabic in every land, and its translations are aids beside it. A Bible read in Malay or Indonesian is a translation whose wording changes with its committee. We set out what the chapter means in our article on Ezekiel 23 and its allegory. Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. Both claims are common in Malaysian and Indonesian debate. The Bismikaa archive discussed the chapter in Kelucahan di dalam Yehezkiel 23.
  2. Ismāʿīl Rājī al-Fārūqī, Al Tawhid: Its Implications for Thought and Life, 2nd ed. (Herndon, VA: International Institute of Islamic Thought, 1992), chapter 2.
  3. Yehezkiel 23:17 and 23:20 in the parallel view of alkitab.sabda.org (Yayasan Lembaga SABDA), read on 26 November 2026: TL (1954), TB (1974), BIS (1985), AYT (2018), Shellabear 2011 and AVB (2015).
  4. Ezekiel 23:20 (World English Bible).
  5. Bryan Bibb, "There's No Sex in Your Violence: Patriarchal Translation in Ezekiel 16 and 23", Review and Expositor 111, no. 4 (2014), pp. 337–345.
